10.1002_aenm.202506154: Although Na‐ and K‐ion batteries are emerging as cost‐effective and sustainable alternatives to Li‐ion batteries (LIBs) for large‐scale energy storage, their distinct physicochemical characteristics present unique challenges in achieving long‐term stability and high electrochemical performance. Among the various performance‐limiting factors, the electrode–electrolyte interphase, including the solid‐electrolyte interphase (SEI) and the cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI), plays a crucial, yet still insufficiently understood, role in determining battery performances. From this perspective, this review offers critical insights into the interphase characteristics, with a special focus on not only clarifying the comparative characteristics of interphases across alkali‐ion battery systems, but also addressing several key issues often overlooked or misunderstood even in LIB research, including: (i) the dynamic and metastable nature of SEI and CEI, (ii) the limitations of fluorine‐rich CEI, (iii) the critical role of binders for interphase optimization, (iv) the overgeneralization of CEI functionality and formation mechanisms, and (v) the impact of interphase stability and passivation on self‐discharge. In doing so, this review emphasizes the pivotal role of interphase design in electrochemical performance, attempts to redefine the so‐called ideal interphases, and highlights the need for a clear and accurate understanding of the fundamental nature and functionalities of the interphases, beyond the conventional definitions, in alkali metal‐ion battery systems.
10.1002_aenm.71511: The commercialization of perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells requires not only scalable processing of the perovskite top cell but also deposition of the different functional layers at rates high enough to enable high‐throughput production. In this work, we bridge the gap between laboratory research and industrial requirements by demonstrating the deposition of hole‐transporting materials, inorganic scaffolds, and electron‐transporting materials at rates at least an order of magnitude higher than conventional baselines using point‐source evaporation. We systematically investigate the impact of accelerated deposition on film properties, composition, and device performance to guide high‐rate processing in industry‐standard scalable tools. By establishing the feasibility of high‐rate evaporation for multiple layers, this study provides realistic insights into the transition from lab‐scale processing of perovskite top cells toward industrial‐scale manufacturing and highlights aspects that have to be considered in the future when switching from laboratory equipment (typically point sources) to industrial equipment (typically linear sources). Through the use of higher evaporation rates for the functional layers, we reached a power conversion efficiency of ~30% in fully textured tandems, increasing to 32.3% with thermally evaporated PDAI passivation. These findings provide crucial insights needed to push perovskite photovoltaic technologies toward high‑throughput and scalable production processes.
10.1021_acsnano.5c20989: Rapid and reliable detection of nanoplastics and other analytes in complex biological and environmental media is very important for public health management and environment protection but there is still a lack of effective methods. Here, we report optoelectronic-tweezer-assisted nanograspers (OET-NGP), a reconfigurable trapping system that dynamically assembles metallic nanoparticles into light-programmable grasping structures. This approach enables not only rapid analyte enrichment but also the formation of highly uniform hotspots with improved Surface-Enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) reproducibility, achieving a detection limit as low as 4.43 × 10 –8 M for Rhodamine B. More importantly, the OET-NGP platform enables in situ capture and SERS detection of nanoplastics at μg/mL level in both aqueous media and serum. These results highlight the capability and great promise of OET-NGP as a powerful sensing tool for effective nanoplastic detection with great potential for environmental monitoring and biosafety assessment.
10.1038_s41467-025-68048-x: Down syndrome, caused by trisomy 21, affects around six million people worldwide and features learning, memory and language deficits. However, the mechanisms underlying trisomy 21 neurophenotypes involving human cortical circuitry are unknown. By characterising developing neural network dynamics and single cell excitability profiles, from synaptic and voltage-dependent ion channel behaviour using an isogenic induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neuronal model, we show that trisomy 21 impairs the activity and development of cortical circuitry. This is caused by deficient glutamatergic synaptic connectivity and by aberrant intrinsic membrane properties involving K + and Na + channels culminating in spike firing defects that weaken neural network activity and disrupt the synchrony of developing neurons. We also identify transiently activated A-type K + channels, specifically Kv4.3 channels, as a key orchestrator for Down syndrome during neurodevelopment. Overall, these excitability changes will significantly contribute towards the aberrant neurophenotypes observed later on in life.
